name: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE)
aliases: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema
symmetrical drug related intertriginous flexural exanthema
symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema

clinicalPearls: Presents as symmetrical, sharply demarcated erythema of the buttocks and perianal or genital area, evoking the historical term baboon syndrome
There is additional symmetrical involvement of at least one other flexural or intertriginous site such as the groins, axillae or antecubital fossae
By definition it follows exposure to a systemic drug, without a preceding external contact allergen at the affected sites
Commonly implicated agents include beta-lactam antibiotics and other antimicrobials, and the reaction often occurs after the first systemic exposure
Characteristically there is an absence of systemic symptoms and no significant fever or organ involvement, distinguishing it from more serious drug reactions
The palms, soles and face are usually spared, and mucosal surfaces are not involved
Histology is non-specific, showing a mild superficial perivascular dermatitis, so diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern and drug history
Management is withdrawal of the responsible drug, after which the eruption settles, with topical corticosteroids to relieve symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is regarded as a systemically induced delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to a drug, without the need for prior sensitisation through skin contact. A systemically administered drug or its metabolite is thought to reach the flexural skin and provoke a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response, with the characteristic predilection for the buttocks and major body folds possibly reflecting local factors such as occlusion, sweat, and a higher density of eccrine structures or drug delivery to these sites. The reaction is confined to the skin, and the lack of systemic features and organ involvement distinguishes it mechanistically from severe cutaneous adverse reactions.
additionalDifferentials: Allergic contact dermatitis to a topical agent
Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis in flexural sites
additionalInvestigations: Detailed systemic drug history correlating exposure with onset
Clinical mapping of the symmetrical flexural and gluteal distribution
Skin swabs or scrapings to exclude candidal, dermatophyte or bacterial intertrigo
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to exclude other flexural dermatoses
Patch and, where appropriate, systemic provocation testing after recovery to confirm the culprit
Assessment for systemic features to exclude a more serious drug reaction
redFlags: Development of pustulation, systemic upset or fever suggesting an alternative severe drug reaction
Mucosal involvement or skin detachment inconsistent with the diagnosis
Failure to settle after drug withdrawal
Signs of secondary infection in the affected folds
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with resolution over one to two weeks once the responsible drug is stopped and no long-term sequelae, although the reaction will recur on re-exposure.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for an infective or inverse-psoriasis intertrigo and missing the drug cause
Failing to recognise that no external contact allergen is required for the flexural eruption
Overlooking that recurrence follows re-exposure to the culprit drug
Confusing it with acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis when pustules develop
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on cutaneous drug reactions
management: Identify and withdraw the responsible systemic drug, often a beta-lactam antibiotic, which is the definitive step
Relieve symptoms with topical corticosteroids and emollients, and antihistamines for pruritus
Document the drug allergy and advise avoidance of the culprit and cross-reactive agents to prevent recurrence
Confirm the culprit where needed with patch testing or supervised provocation after recovery
Reassure the patient given the benign, self-limiting course that settles within a couple of weeks of withdrawal
Assess for systemic features to exclude a more serious cutaneous adverse drug reaction
